title: Koreeda's Monster: A beguiling vision of the split between a dark adult world and a secluded world of light

commenti.body:
> I'm used to the Kore-eda of emotional and subtle dramas like Shoplifters and Nobody Knows, but the first half of this movie felt like something from Yorgos Lanthimos, everyone acting oddly stiff and awkward, like robots. When Minato's mother asked the school principal if she is human, there was a moment where I actually thought it might break out into a sci-fi or thriller in which the school was some kind of cult or alien experiment.

I couldn't disagree with this more. Sakura Ando's performance as Saori was a fantastic depiction of a single mother concerned about her child is met with a stone wall when seeking answers. Yes, the other actors in the scenes with the principal and staff feel scripted and unnatural, but that's _literally the point_ as shown in the perspectives shown later in the film.

> Minato seems to be autistic, and his friend Michitoshi has some developmental issues himself...

This is an extremely out-of-touch, ignorant take on two children playing together, and implies that 5th graders who get along well and play games while not exactly "fitting in" with bullies are mentally disabled. The film clearly shows that Minato was friends even with those bullying Yori, and Yori was dealing with trauma by continuously being physically abused by his alcoholic father for not being straight.

> I think the film is making a commentary about the contrast between the world of judgement, accusations, fear, and mistrust, represented by the adults, and the world of gentle trust and adoration represented by the bond between these children.

This I do generally agree with. I thought it was a very impactful film for all of the reasons you listed. 

> I was puzzled by the structure, but in a way that sparks curiosity, because clearly Kore-eda was trying to say something with it.

I'm not sure if you've seen it or not, but _Monster_ takes a lot of structural inspiration from Akira Kurosawa's 1950 film _Roshomon_. It's an excellent, influential story that aptly gives its name to the _Roshomon effect_, the plot device that _Monster_ utilizes.

Piz, I think we agree more than you think. I understood the point of the principal and staff stonewalling the mother, I just think it was intentionally played in an over the top and exaggerated way to leave you thinking. I thought the scene was great, I was just conveying an actual passing thought I had (that this was a cult or even an alien experiment) due to the absurdity of the school's completely robotic response - which I understand is the point, and I thought that point was made well.

Regarding the 5th graders, I don't think they are mentally disabled. I do think Minato is autistic, or at least somewhere on the autism spectrum, but lots of kids are on the autism spectrum, and I thought it was a great depiction of autism if that is what Kore-eda had in mind. The reason I think he is autistic is primarily because he understands things very literally in a way that is unusual for a kid of any age (I have lots of siblings and nieces and nephews so I'm familiar with developmental stages). The main example is when he takes the idea of a pig brain extremely literally. He also struggles to communicate with his mother in a very basic way that I don't think is normal for neurotypical children. It doesn't have anything to do with him being bullied, and it's no slight against the child or the movie. Similarly, when I say Yori seems to have developmental issues, I am mostly referring to the fact that he has an abusive father and thinks he has a "disease" because he likes boys, and that he isn't capable of standing up for himself - "development issues" was probably a bad way to phrase this. I probably should've said that he has his own struggles. 

My main takeaway, which you said you generally agree with, is about the two worlds in the movie. I'm glad you enjoyed this movie like I did!

>And his reaction by throwing things around the classroom seems typical of kids on the spectrum.

You realize he did that as a distraction, right?

Yes, but I still think it was a strange way to go about doing that. I don't think it was a calculated plan as much as he just felt an urge to somehow make the bullying stop and it sort of burst out of him. But I get that you can interpret it in different ways.

Kore-eda is my favourite director as well and I was lucky enough to see a screening of Monster last week.


The structure definitely makes Monster stand out from Kore-eda's other work, but I would say all the underpinnings are very in line with everything else he's made 


The subtlety and mastery shown in this movie is what really blew me away. Showing you glimpses of actions and character sentiment before completely subverting your understanding and perspective. We do judge the principal for being distant, cold, and unresponsive. But the insight into her life offers context and allows us to empathize. And even in the end, her faults shown throughout the movie aren't entirely reconciled, we don't really know whether she's a good person or not, but we do know that she IS human.


The three retellings do feel extremely isolated from each other even though they are following the same story. I didn't interpret this so much as a separation between adults and children, but rather the feeling of isolation a lot of people feel throughout their life and how that impacts our distrust of others and leads us to judge them unfairly. We dehumanize others to avoid the complexity that lies at the heart of the human experience.


The ambiguity of the ending allows for an uplifting moment even if the reality of the situation is tragic. Personally I interpreted the ending in a straight forward and happy light.


I think this is one of Kore-eda's best, can't wait to rewatch

I don’t think it was too different from his other great movies imo. The structure certainly is different but it touches similar feelings and messages. Thought it was a return to form after his last two.

Yes, the unconventional structure and the tone of the beginning are different, but in the end the themes and the heart are still the same. I watched 11 of his films and it's probably my fourth favorite, after Nobody Knows, Shoplifters, and Like Father Like Son.

Kore-eda's super power is the performances he gets out of the child actors in his movies. this reputation became evident with "Nobody Knows" (2004) but even with his debut - "Maborosi" (1995) - kids have been integral in the stories he tends to tell.

the kids' section, the final one, is the strongest of the three. the movie moves at a slower pace when focused on the two boys and there is less fussing with plot. incidentally, this is the first movie since his debut where Kore-eda did not write the screenplay.

the wild clash of moods in the adult sections - especially in the principal's office - were jarring for me. the mother is pleading in desperation with the staff to be heard and spoken to with empathy and it's devastating. but on the other end, staff people come in and out of that room like it's a farce. this is also true in the hallways where multiple times, the teacher gets led by staff away from the mother. i understand what the movie is going for; the nightmare of this situation is the school has a policy of avoiding confrontation and argument to the point of ridiculousness. but the way it's played and staged, it can't help but resemble comedy - which messes with the dead-serious attitude of the mother.

"Monster" also has one of the best shots Kore-eda has ever captured - the moment when the teacher and the mother are frantically wiping away the grime from the window on the roof of the train car while searching for the boys during the storm. shot from within the train looking up, the drops of rain on the blackness of the dirty window look like stars in a nighttime sky...

Thanks for your thoughts, I agree completely! Nobody Knows is one of my favorite movies and I'd go as far as saying that Kore-eda coached a masterpiece of a performance from Yuya Agira (and the other kids as well). Akira is such a soulful and heartbreaking character. Maborosi is also filled with excellent deep character work, like all of his films. Kore-eda is the master of exploring the delicate intricacies of family relationships. And the last section in Monster is definitely up there with his best work. The gentle depiction of the relationship between the two boys reminds me of Lukas Dhont's Close, which is my favorite film from recent years. I loved the shot you mentioned, as well as the shot of the kids bursting out into the field at the end, and the shot of the burning building with the ambulances racing toward it - I think it was an incredible shot to choose as a centerpiece in the film.

Uhm...I actually don't think it's strange at all and doesn't really indicate any kind of mental/cognitive/developmental issues on his part. Minato >!wanted to protect Yori/stopped the bullying, but he also didn't want the others, especially the bullies to know what he was doing. He had feelings for Yori, and having seen how Yori was relentlessly teased for not behaving like a typical boy, didn't want that (his attraction to Yori) to be found out by anyone or he, too would be teased (which really did happen when he passed the rags to Yori in the third act), so what choice did he have, right? The only thing he could do was to do what he did in that scene: throwing things around to make the bullying stop!<. That's no so much about his mental state and more about >!how constraining the whole situation was for him!< Also while I don't mind you reading any of the characters as neurodivergent, I think you prolly missed the point about Minato >!referring to himself as having a pig's brain. He didn't take it too literally, but you prolly did :). "My brain has been switched with that of a pig" is just his way of conveying to his mom, through a language/metaphor he learned from Yori, that there's something wrong with him/unusual about him!<, and that thing is >!he has feelings for Yori!<. At his age he >!doesn't have the language for describing what's going on with him, same-sex attraction and all that, so he used something metaphorical to try to communicate his struggles!< About Yori, I don't think >!he couldn't stand up for himself bc he's neurodivergent. He was actually quite defiant against the bullies if you pay close attention. He was quite aware of what they're doing to him, what kind of reaction they wanted to provoke!< But >!being smaller and quite alone, there's not much he can do to stop it. Lots of neurotypical kids out there also cant do anything but to just endure bullying, simply because they're outnumbered and no one's helping them. Yori did stand up for himself and fight back, but in an unexpected way: by not playing by the rules of the bullies, by not giving them what they wanted (a reaction: crying, anger, etc.). That's why he acted nonchalantly towards their pranks and refused to say that another female classmate's mole looks like a black bean!<

You make some good arguments and that is a legitimate way to read the characters for sure. I don't and never thought Yori is neurodivergent. It does still seem to me like Minato is on the spectrum, but maybe I was biased from the initial mother perspective before everything is revealed and I need a rewatch. Like for example in the beginning you think Minato is chanting about a monster to himself in a dark tunnel in the middle of nowhere, but later it's revealed he's playing a game with Yori.

Yeah I think you're prolly seeing things >!too much from Saori's perspective :) which I'm sure many are "guilty" of, too :)!< Lots of his actions indeed seemed >!erratic and strange for sure, but when you have all the pieces together, those are just really normal reactions that any kid, neurodivergent or not, would have when experiencing the same struggle as Minato did!<
